Thanks for coming in, Rachel. I read your application, and your track record in luxury sales is impressive.
Thank you. I spent six years at a jewelry house in Chicago, and I recruited and trained most of their sales team.
Good. Let me ask you something practical. Suppose a big client asked for a thirty percent discount. What would you do?
I wouldn't say no right away. I'd ask what the discount is for, and I'd offer something else, like faster delivery.
And imagine you had two important orders on the same day, but only one shipment. Which client would you choose?
The one with the stronger relationship. But I'd call the other client first, before the problem became a surprise.
That's exactly what I want. What would you have done if your old manager had said no to that call?
Honestly, I would have made the call anyway. In sales, I'm accountable for the client, not for my comfort.
One last question. Supposing I offered you the job, when could you start?
In four weeks. And if I'm on your shortlist, I'd love to meet the team in Brazil first.
What would you have done if the client had canceled?
I am looking for someone with a strong track record.
I want a manager who is accountable for results.

Hi Milton, this is Megan from the recruitment agency. Quick update on the export sales manager job. We received sixty applications, and we've put five candidates on the shortlist. Two of them have a strong track record in luxury jewelry, which is rare. My advice for the interviews is simple. Don't only ask people what they did. Ask them what they would do. Suppose a client complained about a late delivery. What would they say? Imagine they had to recruit their own team. Where would they start? The answers tell you much more than an application. One more thing. Turnover in this kind of job is high in New York, around thirty percent a year, so talk about salary early. If we lost a great candidate at the end because of money, it would be a waste for everyone. I'll send you the five profiles tonight.

The worst hire of my career taught me the best lesson. Ten years ago, I recruited a brilliant salesman. Great track record, great energy, great smile. But I never asked him a single hypothetical question. If I had asked him what he would do when a client got angry, I would have seen the problem in five minutes. He didn't like to listen. In the first six months, we lost three good clients. Today I do two things differently. First, I ask every candidate the same question: suppose you made a big mistake with a client, what would you do the next morning? The good ones talk about responsibility. They're accountable. Second, I learned to delegate. A leader who does everything alone builds a team that can't do anything alone. If you want your people to grow, give them real responsibility, and be a mentor, not just a boss.
